result:
Beneath the cracked asphalt of Fourth Avenue, where radiator steam meets the morning cold, the earth still remembers being an ocean. Ten feet down, beneath the tangled fiber cables and iron mains, lies a ribbon of shale stamped with prehistoric ferns. They drank sunlight that burned three hundred million years before the first human thought to stack one brick upon another.

We live so frantically across this upper crust. We measure existence through crowded calendars, delayed subways, and the soft blue glare of battery bars. We curse traffic, entirely forgetting that the limestone forming our curbs was built from the crushed bodies of mollusks who once drifted in warm, sunlit shallows. The city feels permanent, all steel beams, concrete, and glass catching the clouds, yet it is merely a dusting of pollen resting upon the vast sleeve of deep time.

One day, seasonal frost will pry these seams apart. Wandering roots will muscle through empty platforms, drinking cool darkness, and the steel rebar will dissolve into red dust. Steady rains will smooth our proud skyline into rolling, green hills.

There is immense comfort in that slow erasure. Our heavy griefs, our modest ambitions, and our sudden, blazing joys do not need to outlast the stars to matter. They simply need to happen now, here, upon this fragile mantle. We are briefly alive between a forgotten sea and a patient, waiting sky, holding each other’s fleeting hands before the dark earth takes back its quiet stone and rolls on without us.
